title: Related care and considerations
intro: Care that sits alongside gender-affirming hormone therapy: fertility before you start, sexual function, PrEP, and hormones around surgery. It is background reading, not a prescription. Blood tests and reviews are on the [Blood tests and monitoring](#/monitoring) page.

sections.h: Fertility: what to know before you start
body: Hormones can lower fertility, and the loss may be permanent, although there is not enough evidence to say how often. Stopping hormones may bring fertility back, but this is not guaranteed and varies from person to person [1].
Hormones are not contraception. If a pregnancy is possible, contraception is still needed [1].
list: Storing sperm or eggs before starting hormones is an option to talk through with your prescriber [1]
It is not required: you can start hormones without storing sperm or eggs [1]
If you choose to store them, starting hormones may need to wait [1]
Storing eggs and storing sperm differ in cost and in how invasive they are [1]
Adoption is possible in Australia, but it is complex and can take careful planning [1]
sections.note: The [Trans Health SA directory](https://transhealthsa.com/directory/) lists South Australian practitioners, and its listings show which ones offer fertility services.

sections.h: Sexual function on oestrogen and blockers
body: Reduced libido, fewer spontaneous erections and reduced erectile function are recognised effects of oestrogen and androgen blockers. Some people welcome these changes; for others they cause distress [2].
Australia's 2026 standards of care describe the following options, each considered with your prescriber in light of your own goals [2].
list: Reducing the dose of oestrogen or of the androgen blocker, allowing testosterone to rise slightly; this may also bring back some masculinising effects [2]
Sildenafil or tadalafil, which improve erectile function but do not affect libido [2]
Low-dose testosterone after an orchidectomy or when testosterone is fully suppressed, with the dose guided by blood tests [2]
Low-dose testosterone cream applied to the genitals for penile pain associated with oestrogen; the standards note that this is based on clinical experience rather than research [2]
Support from a mental health professional experienced in gender-affirming care, addressing body image and the emotional aspects of sexual function [2]

body: PrEP (pre-exposure prophylaxis) is a medicine that prevents HIV. It does not interact with feminising or masculinising hormones, so the two can be taken together [3].
Australian guidelines suggest that anyone on hormones (including those with a vagina) should take PrEP every day, not only around the time of sex ("on-demand") [3].
PrEP needs regular kidney tests, HIV tests and STI checks. The kidney test matters even more if you also take spironolactone [3].

People often ask whether to stop oestrogen or testosterone before an operation, how long before, and when to restart. The question applies to any surgery, not only gender-affirming surgery: any major operation raises the risk of blood clots (venous thromboembolism) [4].

Australia's 2026 standards of care say there is not enough evidence to stop oestradiol-based therapy routinely around surgery, and that withholding gender-affirming hormones can have significant negative effects. Continuing hormones is particularly important during and after removal of the testes or ovaries (gonadectomy) [4].

Instead, the plan is individual. It weighs your risk of bleeding and of clots against the effects of going without hormones, and it is made with the surgical team. People at intermediate to high clot risk are recommended clot-prevention medicine, and whether to pause hormones is a shared decision based on your own goals [4].

Older Australian guidance differs: the 2019 position statement says oestradiol is typically stopped around the time of surgery to avoid clots, and that a blocker is not needed after an orchidectomy [5].

**Where to read more.** TransHub (ACON) has plain-language pages on each [gender-affirming surgery](https://www.transhub.org.au/trans-folk/#surgeries): facial surgery, orchidectomy, genital reconfiguration surgery, top surgery, breast implants, hysterectomy and vocal surgery. Its [genital reconfiguration surgery page](https://www.transhub.org.au/medical/grs/) notes that some surgeons ask for oestrogen to be reduced for a period before vaginoplasty, and that people with oestradiol implants may time surgery for when blood levels are low. The [Trans Health SA directory](https://transhealthsa.com/directory/) lists South Australian practitioners, including surgeons; it has no surgery information pages.
list: Tell your surgeon and your prescriber about every medicine you take, including any blocker, progesterone, testosterone injection or implant, and PrEP
For blockers, progesterone or implants, ask your surgeon and prescriber what to do around your operation
If you are told to stop a hormone, ask why, for how long, and when you can restart
Do not stop any other medicine unless your surgeon or prescriber asks you to
sections.note: Your surgeon and prescriber decide the plan for your operation together. Costs and referrals for gender-affirming surgery are on the [Resources page](#/resources).
